title: Platform operator handbook: degraded KV and prefix cache mitigation
author: Samir Patel
content:
Overview
========
This runbook describes detection, triage, and mitigation steps when the platform's key-value (KV) cache layer or the prefix-caching proxy exhibits degraded behavior. It focuses on common operational modes for Redwood's inference platform: hosted API traffic, dedicated pools, and private (VPC) deployments. The goal is to restore acceptable latency and cost profiles while minimizing user-visible errors.

Scope
-----
- Services in scope: kv-cache-service (primary in-memory LRU store), prefix-cache-proxy (frontend that implements prefix/KV prefix lookups and TTL logic), routing-service (request routing), and inference-gateway (edge).
- Out of scope: long-term data store corruption, customer-managed on-prem caches (follow customer runbooks).

Owner & stakeholders
---------------------
- Primary oncall owner: Platform SRE rotation (pager: platform-sre@redwood.internal).
- Secondary escalation: Serving Runtime oncall.
- Product/PM notified for customer-impacting incidents.
- Reliability lead: Priya Malhotra.

Background & common failure modes
--------------------------------
KV and prefix caching are used to reduce per-token cost and latency by avoiding repeated model compute for repeated prefixes and frequently requested context. Common failure modes we see in production:
1) Eviction storms: sudden drop in hit-rate due to a large influx of unique keys, often after a rollout or synthetic test.
2) Hotkey amplification: a small set of keys receives huge QPS and causes latency spikes/backpressure in downstream inference pools.
3) Inconsistent TTL/metadata mismatch between prefix-cache-proxy and backing kv-cache-service after a schema or config rollout.
4) Memory leaks or GC stalls in a kv-cache shard (manifest as growth in RSS and long pause times).
5) Network partition / degraded inter-shard communication leading to increased miss rates and retry cascades.

Symptoms & immediate indicators
--------------------------------
- Service-level: 95th/99th percentile request latency for inference-gateway increases by >2x baseline.
- Cache metrics: cache_hit_rate < 70% for >5 minutes (baseline typically 85–95%).
- Hotkey signals: single-key QPS > 10x median tenant QPS or > 200 req/s sustained; increased tail latency on particular key paths.
- Resource metrics: kv-cache-service RSS growth > 20% in 5 minutes or GC pause > 200ms.
- Errors: 5xx from prefix-cache-proxy, increased retry counts in routing-service logs.
- Alerts: CACHE-HIT-RATE-DEGRADATION (SEV2), KV-MEMORY-GROWTH (SEV2), HOTKEY-LATENCY-SPIKE (SEV1 if customer impact).

Impact matrix (quick decision guide)
-----------------------------------
- Tier A (customer-facing errors or broad latency regressions): Activate SEV1. Actions: immediate mitigation, traffic-steering to fallback model variants, page the Serving Runtime oncall.
- Tier B (elevated latency but errors limited to retries): SEV2. Actions: throttles, targeted evictions, configuration rollbacks.
- Tier C (single-shard resource issue with isolated tenants): SEV3. Actions: shard restart, node drain.

Runbook: detection and immediate actions
--------------------------------------
1) Triage: confirm alert source and scope
   - Open the incident channel (#incident-platform-kv).
   - Check Grafana dashboard: "KV Cache — Health & Hotkeys" (dash ID: 8271).
   - Query metrics (Prometheus):
     - cache_hit_rate = sum(cache_hits) / sum(cache_requests) by (pool)
     - kv_rss_bytes and kv_gc_pauses_seconds_count by (instance)
   - Check logs for repeated errors: 
     kubectl -n platform logs deployment/prefix-cache-proxy --since=15m | grep "ERR_CACHE" | tail -n 200

2) Short-term mitigations (select according to severity)
   - Global degraded hit-rate, no memory anomaly: enable conservative routing fallback to bypass prefix-cache-proxy for low-priority tenants. Command: platform-cli routing set-fallback --scope=low --duration=30m --reason="kv-hit-rate-drop"
   - Hotkey detected: enable per-key throttling and local denylist:
     - Add offending key to hotkey-denylist via admin API: POST /admin/hotkeys {"key":"<KEY>","action":"throttle","rate":50} 
     - Apply on both prefix-cache-proxy and routing-service.
   - Memory leak or GC stalls on one shard: drain the shard and restart process:
     - kubectl cordon node <node> && kubectl rollout restart statefulset/kv-cache-service -n platform --selector=shard=<shard-id>
   - TTL mismatch after rollout: temporarily set prefix-cache-proxy config to use legacy TTL mode via the feature-flag service: ffctl set prefix-cache-legacy-ttl true --ttl=30m

3) If latency remains high after short-term mitigation:
   - Activate traffic steering: move 20–40% of traffic for affected routes to dedicated fallback model (model_id: rwd-small-fallback). Use routing-service API: POST /routing/steer {"routes": ["/v1/generate"], "fraction": 0.3, "target":"rwd-small-fallback"} 
   - Notify Customer Success for any tenants whose requests were steered.

4) If errors escalate to SEV1 (widespread 5xx or user-visible failures):
   - Escalate to Serving Runtime and Eng leadership.
   - Consider global rollback of the most recent deploy affecting prefix-cache-proxy or kv-cache-service. Rollback steps depend on deployment type (blue/green vs canary):
     - For canary: platform-cli deploy rollback --service=prefix-cache-proxy --to-tag=<previous-sha>
     - For blue/green: switch traffic to the previous green group in load-balancer (LB control in console).

Operational actions and durable fixes
-----------------------------------
- Increase cache capacity on affected pool (temporary): scale statefulset kv-cache-service replicas to handle hotkey traffic spikes: kubectl scale statefulset/kv-cache-service --replicas=<n> -n platform. Use with caution; this increases memory footprint and cost.
- Apply targeted eviction: via admin API call POST /admin/evict {"prefix":"/user/andy/", "shards": [3,4], "reason":"eviction-during-incident"}
- Roll forward a hotfix (if required) with config changes to prefix-cache-proxy that limit per-key memory allocation to 8MB and enforce LRU smoothing.

Monitoring, dashboards and alert tuning
--------------------------------------
Key dashboards to consult:
- "KV Cache — Health & Hotkeys" (Grafana 8271): hit-rate, per-key QPS heatmap, per-shard memory, GC duration.
- "Routing — Cache Fallbacks" (Grafana 8124): fraction of requests bypassing cache, error budget impact.
- "Platform Overview" (Grafana 8001): top-level latency, errors across services.

Suggested alert thresholds (examples you can tune per pool):
- CACHE-HIT-RATE-DEGRADATION: if cache_hit_rate < 70% for 5 minutes (SEV2).
- HOTKEY-LATENCY-SPIKE: if any key 99th pctl latency > 500ms and key QPS > 200 for 2 minutes (SEV1).
- KV-MEMORY-GROWTH: if rss growth > 25% in 10 minutes or rss > configured_capacity*0.95 (SEV2).
- PREFIX-TTL-MISMATCH: config_hash(prefix-cache-proxy) != config_hash(kv-cache-service) after deploy (SEV2).

Post-incident: root cause analysis and remediation checklist
----------------------------------------------------------
1) Collect artifacts:
   - Grafana snapshots, Prometheus queries, logs from prefix-cache-proxy and kv-cache-service, deployment history, and feature flag changes.
2) RCA template (fill within 48 hours):
   - Title, primary cause, contributing factors, incident timeline, detection gap, mitigation timeline, follow-ups.
3) Follow-up actions (examples):
   - Add pre-deploy TTL compatibility check to CI.
   - Improve per-key throttling algorithm to prefer token-bucket smoothing.
   - Add an automated canary guard that blocks config rollouts which reduce global hit-rate by >5% in canary window.
   - Expand observability: per-tenant cache hit-rate and error tagging.

Testing, drills and runbook validation
------------------------------------
- Quarterly game-day: run synthetic hotkey tests using loadgen (tool: cache-loadgen v1.3) against a sandbox pool. Verify throttling paths and eviction APIs.
- Canary test checklist for prefix-cache-proxy changes:
  1. Deploy to canary pool (2% traffic).
  2. Run synthetic traffic with representative prefix distribution for 30 minutes.
  3. Validate cache_hit_rate delta < 3% and no memory regressions.
  4. Promote on pass, abort and rollback on fail.

Implementation notes & handy references
-------------------------------------
- Admin APIs:
  - POST /admin/hotkeys {key, action, rate}  -- adds or updates hotkey policy
  - POST /admin/evict {prefix, shards, immediate}
  - GET /admin/health  -- returns per-shard health and memory metrics
- Feature flags and config paths:
  - prefix-cache-legacy-ttl (ffctl)
  - kv-cache-max-per-key-bytes (service config, default 16MB)
- CLI snippets:
  - platform-cli metrics query "sum(cache_requests) by (pool)" --from=15m
  - platform-cli routing set-fallback --scope=low --duration=30m --reason="kv-hit-rate-drop"

Example emergency sequence (short-form)
--------------------------------------
1) Alert: CACHE-HIT-RATE-DEGRADATION triggers.
2) Triage: confirm hit-rate drop on Grafana 8271, check for recent deploys.
3) Mitigate: enable routing fallback for low-priority tenants (platform-cli).
4) If hotkey: add offending key to denylist and throttle (admin API).
5) If shard memory: cordon + restart shard.
6) If failure persists: traffic-steer to fallback model and call SEV1.
7) After stabilization: gather artifacts and open an RCA.

Appendix: quick reference table
------------------------------
- Service names: kv-cache-service, prefix-cache-proxy, routing-service, inference-gateway.
- Dashboards: KV Cache 8271, Routing Cache 8124, Platform Overview 8001.
- Common CLI tools: platform-cli, ffctl, kubectl.
- Admin endpoints: /admin/hotkeys, /admin/evict, /admin/health.

Related runbooks and docs
-------------------------
- See platform runbook: predictive-scale-and-eviction-playbook (for capacity control).
- See systems doc: multitenant-workload-slicing-and-queue-demultiplexing (for tenant isolation patterns).

Contact and escalation matrix
-----------------------------
- Platform SRE oncall: platform-sre@redwood.internal (primary)
- Serving Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.internal (secondary)
- Reliability lead: priya.malhotra@redwood.internal
